To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the inhibitor and stimulators of CFU-S are produced locally in different regions of the bone marrow and are spatially separated from each other.
CFU-S proliferation in vivo can be regulated by the production of two soluble factors: one that inhibits and one that stimulates proliferation.

The stem cell is an integral component of the micro-environments in the axial and marginal regions of the marrow, and the stimulator is an integral component in the micro-environment of the fibroblastoid cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms involved in the regulation of the self-renewal of the pluripotent haemopoietic stem cells.
the spatial organisation of the CFU-S proliferation regulatory factors in the marrow.
understanding the mechanisms which regulate the proliferation of the pluripotential stem cell (CFU-S) in the mouse bone marrow and its differentiation into more mature cell types.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CFU-S proliferation is regulated by two distinct factors, an inhibitor which acts on the stem cells themselves and a stimulator whose action is on the differentiation of CFU-S.
the inhibitor is produced by the stromal cells and that the stimulator is produced by the CFU-F.

CFU-S proliferation is maintained by a balance between the stimulator and inhibitor and that the inhibitor is produced by cells in the axial fraction while the stimulator is produced by cells associated with the bone surface.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CFU-S proliferation is regulated by a complex of stimulator and inhibitor molecules, that both of these factors are produced in the bone marrow and that their production is spatially organised.
there are two types of cells which control the proliferation of stem cells.
the CFU-S is maintained in a micro-environment which has a high concentration of an inhibitor-producing cell and a low concentration of a stimulator-producing cell.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the CFU-S proliferation regulator inhibitor and stimulator are produced by different cell types and that these cells are distributed spatially in the marrow in a way that is consistent with the known distribution of CFU-S and CFU-F.
the CFU-S proliferation regulator is not a soluble factor but a cell which can be isolated by its density.
the spatial organisation of the stem cell niche is a key factor in the regulation of stem cell behaviour.
